summary: Teaches length measurement as tiling an object end to end with identical units laid flush, no gaps or overlaps, and reporting the COUNT of those units as the length. Two load-bearing ideas must hold together: units are the same size, and they fill the whole span from one endpoint to the other. The core obstacle is treating measurement as 'put some objects down and count them' — so children leave gaps, mix unit sizes, or start partway along and still confidently read off a number. The Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task captures it: children called a row of 6 short matches 'longer' than 5 long ones because it had more units.
misconceptions: Leaving gaps or overlaps between units but still counting them and reporting a length
Using different-sized units and treating the counts as comparable — concluding the object with MORE units is longer regardless of unit size
Not spanning the whole object — starting the first unit inset from the edge, or stopping before the far end, then counting
Counting the marks/junctions or endpoints rather than the units themselves, producing an off-by-one length

activities.title: Measure a book with paper clips, filling the whole span
steps: Lay identical paper clips along a book, starting flush at one end, so they continue end to end to the far end with no gaps and no overlaps
Run a finger along the book from the very start to the very end to check that the clips cover ALL of it

Report the length as the number of clips that span the book; if the last clip sticks out past the end or a small bit is left that is shorter than a clip, say 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips
Repair a row that someone else laid with obvious gaps or overlaps, nudging the clips flush until the whole span is tiled
Build a small ruler by snapping copies of a single clip into a row, to see that a ruler is just units lined up
activities.insight: A length is the number of equal units that completely fill an object from end to end; gaps, overlaps, or a row that starts inset mean the count does not yet report the true length.

activities.title: Fix the mixed-up puppet's measurement
steps: Look at a row laid by a 'mixed-up' puppet that has visible gaps, overlapping units, or units that start in the middle
Explain what the puppet did wrong
Re-lay the units correctly so they fill the span flush, end to end, with no gaps or overlaps, and give the corrected length
Judge a stated count (e.g. 'I measured this pencil and got 6') against a row that has an obvious gap, and say whether the number is right
activities.insight: A count is only a length when the units completely tile the span; spotting and fixing gaps/overlaps is the child's job, not something to accept on trust.

activities.title: Does 'more units' mean 'longer'? The mixed-size challenge
steps: Measure one object with large clips, then measure the SAME object again with small clips, and compare the two counts
Measure a second object with a jumbled mix of big and small clips, then lay equal-size clips beside it
Answer: 'I measured this ribbon with big clips and got 4, and with little clips I got 8 — did the ribbon get longer? Why did the numbers change?'
Answer: 'Could I measure this with a mix of big and little clips? Why not?'
Optionally run the matches version: compare a row of a few long matches with a row of many short matches that cover the same distance
activities.insight: More units does NOT mean longer when the units are different sizes; the same object gives a bigger count with smaller units without getting any longer, and mixing unit sizes within one measurement makes the count fail to report a length because each unit covers a different amount.

activities.title: Count the units, not the joins
steps: After laying clips along an object, state the count and then point to each thing being counted
Count the units (the clips/spaces), touching each one once, rather than the points where units meet or the end marks
Check a row where the count might be off by one: 'you counted 7 — point to each thing you counted'
activities.insight: The length is the number of units (the spaces covered), not the number of marks or junctions where units meet; counting the joins gives an off-by-one answer.

activities.title: Pick the correct measurement (recognition check)
steps: From several rows laid along an object, choose the one that measures it correctly, where distractors have gaps, overlaps, or mixed-size units
Count the units spanning an object and give the number
Compare two rows that cover the SAME span — a few long units versus many short units — and judge whether the row with more (shorter) units is actually longer, explaining your reasoning
activities.insight: Recognising a valid measurement means checking for full coverage, no gaps/overlaps, and equal units; and when two rows cover the same span, a bigger count made of smaller units does not mean the object is longer.

checkQuestion: Set tasks and WATCH — do not demonstrate first. (1) Give the child a book and a pile of identical paper clips: 'Measure how long the book is.' Watch how they place the clips and how they report the length. (2) Offer a bin that ALSO contains larger and smaller clips mixed in, and ask them to measure a second strip — do they insist on same-size units, or mix them? (3) Show a row you have laid yourself along a pencil with an obvious GAP in the middle (and count aloud a number): 'I measured this pencil and got 6. Is that right?' Watch whether the child spots that gaps/overlaps or mixed units make the count wrong.
checkAnswer: (1) Lays identical clips end to end, flush at one end of the book, with no gaps or overlaps, spanning the whole book, and states the length as the number of clips. (2) Uses only same-size clips (or points out that the sizes must match) and explains that mixing sizes makes the counts unfair. (3) Says the gappy measure is wrong because the clips do not cover the whole pencil with no gaps — the count only gives the length when the units fully tile the span.
